Thus final answer: \boxed{a=m^2-n^2,\ b=m^2+2mn,\ c=m^2+mn+n^2}.<|end_think|>From the law of cosines for a \(60^{\circ }\) angle we have  

\[
c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-ab .
\tag{1}
\]

Multiplying (1) by \(4\) gives  

\[
(2c)^{2}=(2a-b)^{2}+3b^{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

Equation (2) is the analogue of the Pythagorean equation in the ring of
Eisenstein integers \(\mathbb Z[\omega]\) \((\omega=e^{i\pi/3})\), whose norm is  

\[
N(x+y\omega)=x^{2}-xy+y^{2}.
\]

If we write  

\[
u=2c+2a-b,\qquad v=2c-2a+b,
\]

then (2) becomes  

\[
u\,v=3b^{2}.
\tag{3}
\]

Since \(\gcd(u,v)=\gcd(u+v,\,u-v)=\gcd(4c,4a-2b)\) is a divisor of \(2\), the only
possibility for a primitive solution of (3) is  

\[
u=3m^{2},\qquad v=n^{2},\qquad b=mn,
\]

with positive integers \(m>n\).  Substituting these expressions into the
definitions of \(u\) and \(v\) and solving for \(a\) and \(c\) yields  

\[
\begin{aligned}
2c+2a-b &=3m^{2},\\[2pt]
2c-2a+b &=n^{2},
\end{aligned}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\begin{cases}
a=m^{2}-n^{2},\\[2pt]
b=m^{2}+2mn,\\[2pt]
c=m^{2}+mn+n^{2}.
\end{cases}
\]

One checks directly that these satisfy (1):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a^{2}+b^{2}-ab
&=(m^{2}-n^{2})^{2}+(m^{2}+2mn)^{2}-(m^{2}-n^{2})(m^{2}+2mn)\\
&=(m^{2}+mn+n^{2})^{2}=c^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus every integer triangle with a \(60^{\circ}\) angle between sides
\(a\) and \(b\) can be expressed (up to a common factor) by the
parameterisation

\[
\boxed{a=m^{2}-n^{2},\qquad b=m^{2}+2mn,\qquad c=m^{2}+mn+n^{2}},
\qquad m,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\; m>n .
\]<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
